# Git Repository: Backup, Sync & Update

## When to use

- User asks to "update from Git" / "pull latest" / sync a local clone.
- A remote branch was force-pushed and a normal `pull --ff-only` fails with "diverging branches".
- GitHub/HTTPS fetches fail with OpenSSL/TLS errors.
- **User asks whether work is backed up ("备份到 git 了吗"). Run the audit below before answering — never answer from memory or from the presence of a `.gitignore`.**

## Is it even a repo? (audit before answering "backed up")

Do not infer a repo from a `.gitignore`, a `files` whitelist, or commits elsewhere in the tree. **A well-commented `.gitignore` with no `.git` is a real observed state** — someone intended to init and never did. Walk up from the project dir to the drive root:

```powershell
$p='D:\path\to\proj'
while ($p) { if (Test-Path (Join-Path $p '.git')) { "repo at $p"; break }
             $n=Split-Path $p -Parent; if ($n -eq $p -or -not $n) { 'NO repo up to drive root'; break }; $p=$n }
```

Check all three backup forms, not just the first:

| form | check |
|---|---|
| local repo | walk-up above |
| remote, actually synced | `git remote -v`; `rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD` **and** `HEAD..origin/main` both 0 |
| published artifact | `npm view <name> version` — empty means never published |

Also search the disk for a second copy before concluding; the directory can be the only one.

**Quantify what is NOT covered — "it ships" and "it is backed up" are different sets.** A published tarball is a whitelist subset; measure it:

```bash
npm pack --dry-run                              # text mode: "total files" + the file list
node -e "console.log(require('./package.json').files)"
```

Real case: whitelist `["index.js","client.js","lib/","cordis.patch.yml","README.md","USAGE.md"]` = 19 files / 239 kB shipped, while `design/` (24 docs), `test/`, `tools/`, `SMOKE.md` — **84% of the project by volume, and the least reproducible part** — sat on one disk with zero copies.

## Establishing the repo (when the audit finds none)

1. **Read the committer identity from an existing repo's LOCAL config — do not invent one, and do not assume a global one exists.**
   ```bash
   git -C <an-existing-repo> config --local user.name
   git -C <an-existing-repo> config --local user.email
   ```
   On this machine global `user.name`/`user.email` were **empty** while several repos had commits, because each set it locally. Copy that value; set it `--local` on the new repo.
2. `git init -b main`, then `git add -A` and **inspect the staged set before committing**: assert 0 hits for `node_modules`, scratch dirs, and anything the `.gitignore` exists to catch.
3. Work-in-progress defaults to private: `gh repo create <name> --private --source <dir> --remote origin --push`.
4. **Verify by fetching the content back, not by the push exit code.**

## Verifying a backup is real

A successful `push`, and `ls-remote` matching the local SHA, only prove a **ref** moved. **A fresh clone into an independent directory is the proof**, because it re-downloads the objects:

```bash
git clone --quiet <url> /tmp/verify-clone
git -C /tmp/verify-clone ls-files | wc -l     # == local tracked count
git -C /tmp/verify-clone rev-parse HEAD       # == local HEAD sha
```
Spot-check that known-large files exist with plausible byte sizes, confirm no `node_modules`/scratch leakage, then delete the clone.

**SUSPECT THE EXTRACTOR when a verification count comes back 0.** Two false zeros in one session, both from the *measurement*, not the repo:

- `gh api <url> --jq '...'` printed nothing ⇒ looked like an empty repo. Bare `gh api <url>` exited 0 with full JSON; the `--jq` invocation was at fault.
- `npm pack --dry-run --json | ConvertFrom-Json` yielded 0 files ⇒ looked like an empty tarball. Plain `npm pack --dry-run` listed 19.

Rule: on a 0 or empty result, re-run the same check with the **dumbest possible output** (no `--jq`, no `--json`, no filtering) before believing it. A zero that would be alarming is far more often a broken extractor than a broken world.

> Real case with numbers, commands and transcripts: `references/backup-gap-audit.md`.

## Safe update workflow

1. Inspect before changing anything:
   ```bash
   git status --short --branch
   git remote -v
   git log --oneline --decorate -5
   ```
2. Prefer a fast-forward pull:
   ```bash
   git pull --ff-only
   ```
   - If it fails only due to SSL, see below and retry with the same command plus the workaround.
   - If it says "Not possible to fast-forward", do **not** assume it is safe to force-reset immediately. Check whether local work is uncommitted and whether local `main` was merely the previous remote tip.
3. For a clean worktree where the remote was force-pushed:
   - Create a backup ref so the operation is reversible:
     ```bash
     git branch backup/main-pre-update
     ```
   - Fetch the real remote state:
     ```bash
     git fetch origin
     ```
   - Point the branch at the remote:
     ```bash
     git reset --hard origin/main
     ```
   - Verify:
     ```bash
     git status --short --branch
     git log -1 --oneline --decorate
     ```
   - Tell the user how to restore if needed:
     ```bash
     git reset --hard backup/main-pre-update
     ```
4. If there are local uncommitted changes or local-only commits that matter, do **not** hard reset automatically. Merge or rebase carefully, or ask the user.

## GitHub/HTTPS connectivity workarounds

On some Windows/proxied environments, `git pull` may fail with:

```text
OpenSSL SSL_connect: SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL in connection to github.com:443
```

Retry with both of these Git options (they work together for this failure mode):

```bash
git -c http.sslVerify=false -c http.version=HTTP/1.1 pull --ff-only
```

For read-only checks first:

```bash
git -c http.sslVerify=false -c http.version=HTTP/1.1 ls-remote --heads origin
```

Notes:
- Do not treat this as permanent "GitHub is broken". The same command often succeeds after tweaking HTTP version/TLS verification.

**First settle WHICH ROUTE is live — never reason from a belief about it.** The same
machine can present the mirror image: the configured proxy works while the direct route
is dead. Measured in one session, both aimed at `127.0.0.1:7897`:

- `git ls-remote --heads origin` (**through** the configured proxy) → **exit 0**, returned
  the ref
- `git -c http.proxy= -c https.proxy= ls-remote --heads origin` (**bypass**) → **exit 128**,
  `Failed to connect to github.com port 443 after 21089 ms: Couldn't connect to server`

So run both — one cheap line each — and use whichever exits 0:

```bash
git ls-remote --heads origin
git -c http.proxy= -c https.proxy= ls-remote --heads origin
```

**The bypass is a mode you may be carrying, not a cure.** Putting `-c http.proxy=` on
every command is what turned eight consecutive pushes into 21-second timeouts: the flag
had been inherited from an earlier round in which the proxy *was* the broken hop. Re-test
the direction each time instead of reusing last time's answer, and leave the owner's git
config alone either way.

**A transport error with a ~21 s timeout means the route is dead, not the repo.** Two
signatures, same meaning: `OpenSSL SSL_connect: SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL`, and
`Failed to connect to github.com port 443 ... Couldn't connect to server`.

**Read the output, not only the exit code.** A failed push printed
`Everything up-to-date` while returning non-zero; reading that line as "nothing to do"
hid a whole round of failed pushes. Output that contradicts the exit status is a fact to
chase immediately.

**Check whether the proxy is even running before retrying.** On this machine
the proxy is Clash on `127.0.0.1:7897`, and it is only listening while the
Clash app is up. With Clash off, `git clone/ls-remote/fetch` over HTTPS fails
as `OpenSSL SSL_connect: SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL`, and **no git-side flag fixes it** —
verbatim failures observed in one session:

- `-c http.sslVerify=false -c http.version=HTTP/1.1` → `SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL`
- `-c http.sslBackend=schannel` → `schannel: failed to receive handshake`
- `-c http.proxy=http://127.0.0.1:7897` (explicit instead of env var) → `SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL`

Five retries with backoff all failed; the same command succeeded on the first
try after the user started Clash. So: if two attempts fail this way, stop
retrying and ask the user to start Clash, then run it once.

Triage asymmetry worth knowing: while git was failing, `gh api` and
`npm view` still succeeded over the same proxy. A working `gh` therefore does
NOT mean git will work — the transport differs, not the network.
- If the issue is a mid-transfer drop, retry after a short wait; an external proxy can be selective per host.
- You may set these flags only for the command, or persist them with `git config --global` if this environment routinely needs them.

## Diagnostics when a pull aborts

- `git branch -a -vv` shows ahead/behind counts.
- `git merge-base main origin/main` shows whether histories truly diverged.
- A forced update appears in fetch output as:
  ```text
  + <old>...<new> main -> origin/main (forced update)
  ```
- If local `main` exactly equals the old remote `main` and the worktree is clean, resetting to `origin/main` is normally the correct "update" action.

## Verification

After update, confirm:
- `git status --short --branch` shows no ahead/behind (or intended state).
- `git log -1 --oneline --decorate` shows `HEAD -> main, origin/main`.
- If a backup branch was created, list it: `git branch --list 'backup/*'`.

## Mirroring a very large repository (thousands of refs)

Real case (2026), `openclaw/openclaw`: 7110 branch heads, 747 tags, 99,267 commits on `main`, 5,007,620 objects.

- Prefer ONE `git clone --mirror`. Sliced fetching (`--depth=1000` then repeated `--deepen=2000`) cost ~3x the space of a single pack: 11k commits already occupied 2.2 GB while `main` alone has ~99k commits.
- Expect roughly 75-100 s of TOTAL SILENCE before the first byte: GitHub builds the pack server-side. Silence is not a stall.
- Do NOT judge progress by the pack file or `objects/pack` size:
  - a running clone writes the pack as `objects/pack/tmp_pack_*`, which `git count-objects -vH` reports under `garbage`;
  - that file can be invisible to `Get-ChildItem` while git holds it open, so a size probe reads 0 forever.
  Use git's own `--progress` output, or watch free disk space.
- Never kill a transfer on a "no size change" heuristic; a broken detector killed a healthy clone at 11%.
- Killing the parent `git` does NOT stop the transfer. `git-remote-https` / `index-pack` children keep running, keep the tmp pack and the redirected log locked, and become zombies that block a re-clone. Kill the whole tree: `taskkill /PID <pid> /T /F`.
- Do not run two GitHub transfers at once through the same proxy. Contention appears as `RPC failed; curl 56 ... SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL` during ref listing — a proxy symptom that looks like a repo problem.
- Settings that worked on Windows through a local proxy: `HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:7897`, `-c http.sslVerify=false -c http.version=HTTP/1.1`, plus `-c http.lowSpeedLimit=1000 -c http.lowSpeedTime=600` as a genuine-stall guard.
- Wipe a failed target properly: kill git first, `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force`, fall back to `cmd /c rmdir /s /q`, then ASSERT the path is gone. `git clone` refuses a non-empty destination ("destination path already exists") and fails in seconds.

Progress tail that survives the `\r`-only progress stream and locked files:

```powershell
$fs=[System.IO.File]::Open($err,'Open','Read','ReadWrite')
$sr=New-Object System.IO.StreamReader($fs); $raw=$sr.ReadToEnd(); $sr.Close(); $fs.Close()
($raw -split [char]13) | Where-Object { $_.Trim() } | Select-Object -Last 1
```

Verifying a finished mirror (mirror the remote's own numbers, not assumptions):

```bash
git -C repo.git for-each-ref --format='%(refname)' refs/heads | wc -l    # == remote head count
git -C repo.git for-each-ref --format='%(refname)' refs/tags  | wc -l    # == remote tag count
git -C repo.git rev-parse 'refs/tags/vX.Y.Z^{commit}'                    # == remote tag commit
git -C repo.git rev-parse --is-bare-repository --is-shallow-repository   # true false
git -C repo.git count-objects -vH                                        # size-pack sane, garbage 0
```

## Related reference

- `references/backup-gap-audit.md` — the "is it backed up?" audit end to end: walk-up check, the four commands and their exact output, the 84%-unbacked set difference, identity-from-local-config, private-remote creation, fresh-clone verification, and the two false zeros.
- `references/github-ssl-and-force-push-case.md` — a real-case walkthrough (2026) with SSL workaround, forced-update diagnosis, backup branch, and reset.

> Real case with numbers, commands and transcripts: `references/backup-gap-audit.md`.

## Safe update workflow

1. Inspect before changing anything:
   ```bash
   git status --short --branch
   git remote -v
   git log --oneline --decorate -5
   ```
2. Prefer a fast-forward pull:
   ```bash
   git pull --ff-only
   ```
   - If it fails only due to SSL, see below and retry with the same command plus the workaround.
   - If it says "Not possible to fast-forward", do **not** assume it is safe to force-reset immediately. Check whether local work is uncommitted and whether local `main` was merely the previous remote tip.
3. For a clean worktree where the remote was force-pushed:
   - Create a backup ref so the operation is reversible:
     ```bash
     git branch backup/main-pre-update
     ```
   - Fetch the real remote state:
     ```bash
     git fetch origin
     ```
   - Point the branch at the remote:
     ```bash
     git reset --hard origin/main
     ```
   - Verify:
     ```bash
     git status --short --branch
     git log -1 --oneline --decorate
     ```
   - Tell the user how to restore if needed:
     ```bash
     git reset --hard backup/main-pre-update
     ```
4. If there are local uncommitted changes or local-only commits that matter, do **not** hard reset automatically. Merge or rebase carefully, or ask the user.

## GitHub/HTTPS connectivity workarounds

On some Windows/proxied environments, `git pull` may fail with:

```text
OpenSSL SSL_connect: SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL in connection to github.com:443
```

Retry with both of these Git options (they work together for this failure mode):

```bash
git -c http.sslVerify=false -c http.version=HTTP/1.1 pull --ff-only
```

For read-only checks first:

```bash
git -c http.sslVerify=false -c http.version=HTTP/1.1 ls-remote --heads origin
```

Notes:
- Do not treat this as permanent "GitHub is broken". The same command often succeeds after tweaking HTTP version/TLS verification.

**First settle WHICH ROUTE is live — never reason from a belief about it.** The same
machine can present the mirror image: the configured proxy works while the direct route
is dead. Measured in one session, both aimed at `127.0.0.1:7897`:

- `git ls-remote --heads origin` (**through** the configured proxy) → **exit 0**, returned
  the ref
- `git -c http.proxy= -c https.proxy= ls-remote --heads origin` (**bypass**) → **exit 128**,
  `Failed to connect to github.com port 443 after 21089 ms: Couldn't connect to server`

So run both — one cheap line each — and use whichever exits 0:

```bash
git ls-remote --heads origin
git -c http.proxy= -c https.proxy= ls-remote --heads origin
```

**The bypass is a mode you may be carrying, not a cure.** Putting `-c http.proxy=` on
every command is what turned eight consecutive pushes into 21-second timeouts: the flag
had been inherited from an earlier round in which the proxy *was* the broken hop. Re-test
the direction each time instead of reusing last time's answer, and leave the owner's git
config alone either way.

**A transport error with a ~21 s timeout means the route is dead, not the repo.** Two
signatures, same meaning: `OpenSSL SSL_connect: SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL`, and
`Failed to connect to github.com port 443 ... Couldn't connect to server`.

**Read the output, not only the exit code.** A failed push printed
`Everything up-to-date` while returning non-zero; reading that line as "nothing to do"
hid a whole round of failed pushes. Output that contradicts the exit status is a fact to
chase immediately.

**Check whether the proxy is even running before retrying.** On this machine
the proxy is Clash on `127.0.0.1:7897`, and it is only listening while the
Clash app is up. With Clash off, `git clone/ls-remote/fetch` over HTTPS fails
as `OpenSSL SSL_connect: SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL`, and **no git-side flag fixes it** —
verbatim failures observed in one session:

- `-c http.sslVerify=false -c http.version=HTTP/1.1` → `SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL`
- `-c http.sslBackend=schannel` → `schannel: failed to receive handshake`
- `-c http.proxy=http://127.0.0.1:7897` (explicit instead of env var) → `SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL`

Five retries with backoff all failed; the same command succeeded on the first
try after the user started Clash. So: if two attempts fail this way, stop
retrying and ask the user to start Clash, then run it once.

Triage asymmetry worth knowing: while git was failing, `gh api` and
`npm view` still succeeded over the same proxy. A working `gh` therefore does
NOT mean git will work — the transport differs, not the network.
- If the issue is a mid-transfer drop, retry after a short wait; an external proxy can be selective per host.
- You may set these flags only for the command, or persist them with `git config --global` if this environment routinely needs them.

## Diagnostics when a pull aborts

- `git branch -a -vv` shows ahead/behind counts.
- `git merge-base main origin/main` shows whether histories truly diverged.
- A forced update appears in fetch output as:
  ```text
  + <old>...<new> main -> origin/main (forced update)
  ```
- If local `main` exactly equals the old remote `main` and the worktree is clean, resetting to `origin/main` is normally the correct "update" action.

After update, confirm:
- `git status --short --branch` shows no ahead/behind (or intended state).
- `git log -1 --oneline --decorate` shows `HEAD -> main, origin/main`.
- If a backup branch was created, list it: `git branch --list 'backup/*'`.

## Mirroring a very large repository (thousands of refs)

Real case (2026), `openclaw/openclaw`: 7110 branch heads, 747 tags, 99,267 commits on `main`, 5,007,620 objects.

- Prefer ONE `git clone --mirror`. Sliced fetching (`--depth=1000` then repeated `--deepen=2000`) cost ~3x the space of a single pack: 11k commits already occupied 2.2 GB while `main` alone has ~99k commits.
- Expect roughly 75-100 s of TOTAL SILENCE before the first byte: GitHub builds the pack server-side. Silence is not a stall.
- Do NOT judge progress by the pack file or `objects/pack` size:
  - a running clone writes the pack as `objects/pack/tmp_pack_*`, which `git count-objects -vH` reports under `garbage`;
  - that file can be invisible to `Get-ChildItem` while git holds it open, so a size probe reads 0 forever.
  Use git's own `--progress` output, or watch free disk space.
- Never kill a transfer on a "no size change" heuristic; a broken detector killed a healthy clone at 11%.
- Killing the parent `git` does NOT stop the transfer. `git-remote-https` / `index-pack` children keep running, keep the tmp pack and the redirected log locked, and become zombies that block a re-clone. Kill the whole tree: `taskkill /PID <pid> /T /F`.
- Do not run two GitHub transfers at once through the same proxy. Contention appears as `RPC failed; curl 56 ... SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL` during ref listing — a proxy symptom that looks like a repo problem.
- Settings that worked on Windows through a local proxy: `HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:7897`, `-c http.sslVerify=false -c http.version=HTTP/1.1`, plus `-c http.lowSpeedLimit=1000 -c http.lowSpeedTime=600` as a genuine-stall guard.
- Wipe a failed target properly: kill git first, `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force`, fall back to `cmd /c rmdir /s /q`, then ASSERT the path is gone. `git clone` refuses a non-empty destination ("destination path already exists") and fails in seconds.

Progress tail that survives the `\r`-only progress stream and locked files:

```powershell
$fs=[System.IO.File]::Open($err,'Open','Read','ReadWrite')
$sr=New-Object System.IO.StreamReader($fs); $raw=$sr.ReadToEnd(); $sr.Close(); $fs.Close()
($raw -split [char]13) | Where-Object { $_.Trim() } | Select-Object -Last 1
```

Verifying a finished mirror (mirror the remote's own numbers, not assumptions):

```bash
git -C repo.git for-each-ref --format='%(refname)' refs/heads | wc -l    # == remote head count
git -C repo.git for-each-ref --format='%(refname)' refs/tags  | wc -l    # == remote tag count
git -C repo.git rev-parse 'refs/tags/vX.Y.Z^{commit}'                    # == remote tag commit
git -C repo.git rev-parse --is-bare-repository --is-shallow-repository   # true false
git -C repo.git count-objects -vH                                        # size-pack sane, garbage 0
```

# InkOS Novel-Writing Harness (local)

## What it is

- CLI: `inkos`, from global npm package `@actalk/inkos` (AGPL-3.0, source: https://github.com/Narcooo/inkos).
- Multi-agent novel production: Writer → Validator → Auditor → Reviser with human review gates. Supports long-form fiction, shorts, fanfic, continuations, covers, interactive worlds, translation, AUDIT/revise pipelines.
- Companion packages: `@actalk/inkos-core`, `@actalk/inkos-studio`; total install is large (~485 MB for @actalk/inkos alone).

## Key locations (Windows/Git Bash)

| Item | Path |
|---|---|
| Global npm package | `C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\npm\node_modules\@actalk\inkos` |
| CLI shim | `C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\npm\inkos.cmd` |
| Global LLM config | `~/.inkos/.env` — `INKOS_LLM_PROVIDER/BASE_URL/API_KEY/MODEL` |
| Codemoss skill link | `~/.codemoss/skills/global/inkos-multi-agent-novel-writing` → `~/.cc-switch/skills/inkos-multi-agent-novel-writing` |
| Skill source repo | https://github.com/Aradotso/trending-skills, path `skills/inkos-multi-agent-novel-writing/SKILL.md` |
| Project file | `./inkos.json` (created by `inkos init` or auto-initialized by Studio) |

## Quick verification

```bash
inkos --version
inkos doctor          # checks Node >= 20, global config, API connectivity (consumes a few LLM tokens)
```

## Common commands

- `inkos init [name]` — create a project in the current directory (`inkos.json`)
- `inkos studio [-p <port>]` — start the InkOS Studio web workbench (default port 4567)
- `inkos book / chapter / write / review / status / export / audit / revise / plan / compose`
- `inkos auto <book-id> <target-chapter>` — autonomous chapter writing
- `inkos tui` — terminal workspace; `inkos up` / `down` — daemon mode
- `inkos doctor --repair-node-runtime` — write pinned `.nvmrc` / `.node-version`

## Starting Studio reliably

- Run it **from the project directory**. If no `inkos.json` exists in cwd, Studio auto-initializes a minimal project **in the current directory** — in Git Bash, `/tmp` maps to Windows `%TEMP%`, so avoid launching from there unless intentional.
- Detached start:
  ```bash
  cd /path/to/project
  nohup /c/Users/<user>/AppData/Roaming/npm/inkos.cmd studio -p 4567 > /tmp/inkos-studio.log 2>&1 &
  ```
- Verify:
  ```bash
  netstat -ano | grep ":4567"
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1:4567/   # expect 200
  ```
- Log file: `/tmp/inkos-studio.log` (when launched from Git Bash).

## Restore a broken codemoss skill link

Symptom: `~/.cc-switch/skills` vanished, so `~/.codemoss/skills/global/*` symlinks are all BROKEN. Restore just InkOS skill:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.cc-switch/skills/inkos-multi-agent-novel-writing
curl -fsSL -o ~/.cc-switch/skills/inkos-multi-agent-novel-writing/SKILL.md \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Aradotso/trending-skills/main/skills/inkos-multi-agent-novel-writing/SKILL.md
```

Validate: `ls -la ~/.codemoss/skills/global/inkos-multi-agent-novel-writing/` lists `SKILL.md`.

## Notes

- `inkos doctor` may print `LLM API Key: Missing` while the global config still works (it wants a Studio service key); the `API Connectivity: OK` line is the practical validity test.
- Project-level `.env` / `.nvmrc` missing is expected before `inkos init` completes setup.
- LLM calls consume real tokens; confirm before bulk `auto` / daemon runs.

# Invention Point Mining

Turn a codebase into a graded list of candidate invention points, each backed by
file:line evidence and a prior-art verdict. It does NOT draft patent
applications, does not search patent databases, and needs nothing beyond
git/grep/npm plus the ability to read the repo. The output is an assessment the
user takes to a patent attorney or an in-house filing pipeline.

## When to Use

- "这个项目有哪些可以写进专利的技术点？"
- "这些技术点能不能水专利 / 能撑独权吗？"
- "按照同样的口径分析另一个项目" — repeat the sweep on a sibling repo.
- Framing an application whose subject matter is a domain (e.g. skills) and needs
  scenario-level dependent claims written alongside other material.

## Prerequisites

- The target repo path, and if it is a port: the upstream/reference repo it came
  from (novelty is decided relative to that).
- `git` for remote/history, and npm for publication status.
- On PowerShell, `npm` resolves to `npm.ps1` and can be blocked by execution
  policy — call `npm.cmd` through `cmd /c`.

## How to Run

1. Recon + novelty probes (Quick Reference).
2. Evidence sweep: parallel subagents for the big packages, and read the small
   decisive files yourself (validators, state machines, registries, seams).
3. Grade every candidate S / A / B / OFF.
4. Assemble the claim tree and the "do not touch" prior-art list.
5. Deliver per point: scenario → failure mode → feature chain (file:line) →
   effect, plus collision risk and the experiment that would prove the effect.
   Hand over the outline first, then write.

## Quick Reference

Three gates — a point failing any gate is not writable:

| Gate | Rule | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Type | CN utility models protect products only | methods/software ⇒ invention patent only |
| Subject | Art. 25 excludes mental rules | need technical problem → technical means → technical effect on system resources |
| Novelty | the applicant's own prior publication destroys it | check git remote, npm versions, first-commit date |

Four-part frame per point: 场景 → 系统层失效模式 → 特征链 → 可量化效果.

Grades: **S** independent claim · **A** dependent claim · **B** embodiment only ·
**OFF** prior art (background section at most).

Novelty probes:

```bash
git remote -v
git log --reverse --format='%ci %s' -1; git log -1 --format='%ci %s'
cmd /c "npm.cmd view <pkg> versions --json"        # PowerShell-safe
grep -rn "<same-concept-synonyms>" <reference-repo>  # 0 hits = novel candidate
```

## Procedure

1. **Recon.** Root docs, package list, LOC per package, test layout. Docs are
   leads, never evidence.
2. **Novelty probes.** `git remote -v` + `npm view` + first/last commit dates
   decide whether the code is already public. Published code is prior art
   against a later filing — CN has no general grace period.
3. **Split novel from aligned.** Read the target implementation (file:line), then
   grep the reference repo for the same concept. Aligned ⇒ prior art. Keep
   grepping until an absence is a real absence, and record the greps used.
4. **Separate platform-given from plugin-given.** Check the platform repo for an
   equivalent API (injection point, approval seam, cache boundary). A wrapper
   over a platform capability is not an invention point.
5. **Grade.** S: a system-level failure mode + specific means + measurable
   effect. A: same shape, narrower or weaker novelty. B: real mechanism but
   plumbing. OFF: already in the upstream or the platform.
6. **Assemble.** Name the one specific technical feature every independent claim
   shares (unity), put S points as independent claims, A points as dependent
   claims grouped by usage scenario.
7. **Bucket the slices S / A / B / 别碰 — never letter the lifecycle stages.**
   The grade vocabulary is the skeleton of the answer; an earlier draft used
   A–F for stages and the grades disappeared. See
   `references/skill-scenario-catalog.md`.
8. **State each slice on the FUNCTIONAL side of a concrete scenario.**
   Read it as: 场景（谁在做什么）→ 系统做了什么（用户看得见的行为）→
   可观察结果; the failure mode and the mechanism (lock / anchor / state
   machine / cache) are the supporting evidence and the writability
   justification, never the headline.
9. **Deliver as scenario slices, not as a novelty ranking.** The user's
   application is ONE domain filing (e.g. skills) that also carries outside
   material, so each point is a slice: 场景 / 系统层失效模式 / 特征链 (file:line) /
   独权-从权-实施例 / 前置与验收. Never present the sweep as a list of separate
   filings; see `references/skill-scenario-catalog.md` for the delivered shape.

## Pitfalls

- **Docs drift from code.** Measured: a repo's own audit table claimed 9 hooks and
  5 prompt skills; the code had 11 and 4. Verify every claim against source.
- **"Concept exists upstream" ≠ "implementation identical."** When the concept is
  upstream but the mechanism differs (different event model, different state
  machine, different failure handling), write it as a dependent claim and put
  the difference into the features.
- **Thresholds, constants, prompt text and config plumbing are not inventions.**
- Gate/CI/build-tooling mechanisms (guards, generators, drift detectors, install
  state machines) count only when the filing is anchored on that pipeline; for a
  runtime-anchored filing record them as B-tier and move on.
- A port or an open-sourced project makes everything aligned with its parent
  prior art; only the host-specific engineering survives.
- **Never invent experimental data.** Ship the effect claim plus the experiment
  list instead.
- Raise own-publication ordering and employee-invention ownership before
  promising anything.

## Verification

- Every S/A point cites file:line that `read` can open.
- Every "novel" claim reproduces with the same absence grep against the reference
  repo.
- The deliverable contains a "do not touch" list; without it the sweep was not
  exhaustive.

## References

- `references/disclosure-docx-house-style.md` — the house style of the user's
  existing 交底书 files, and the recipe for emitting a .docx that inherits the
  template's styles (python-docx is available; template-as-container).
- `references/cn-invention-patent-rubric.md` — CN legal gates, claim-tree rules,
  common rejection grounds, 交底书 checklist.
- `references/worked-examples.md` — two graded sweeps (hermes-claw,
  dsh-evolution) reusable as a prior map.

# Literature Artifact Triage

Builds a filtered, evidence-graded literature list: find papers matching stated inclusion
criteria, then **verify each claimed artifact and each author affiliation** before ranking.
It does NOT write the papers' science, and it does not rank by citation counts or popularity.
Core stance: rank by *what you can actually obtain*, not by what the paper claims to release.

## When to Use

- "Find research on X since <date>, prioritize high-quality / reliable authors / with GitHub or HuggingFace links"
- "Which of these papers can I actually reproduce?"
- Any request where a paper's *artifact availability* or *author credibility* is a selection criterion.
- Also use when auditing a report someone else produced for unsupported artifact claims.

## Prerequisites

None. Uses `web_search`, `web_fetch`, `subagent`, `skill_manage`. For arXiv metadata prefer the
Atom API (`https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?...`) — it returns authors, dates, `journal_ref`
and the full abstract in one call.

## Quick Reference

| Need | Call |
|---|---|
| Paper metadata (authors, venue, dates) | `export.arxiv.org/api/query?id_list=<ids>&max_results=N` |
| Metadata for a whole list at once | ONE `id_list=` request carrying every ID (`max_results=100`) — splitting into small batches trips `Rate exceeded.` (HTTP 429); on 429 wait ~60 s and retry the same single call |
| Survey PDF → text | bundled Python has `pypdf`: `PdfReader(p).pages[i].extract_text()` per page, keep `=== PAGE n ===` markers |
| Artifact verdict for a whole list | `node scripts/verify-paper-artifacts.mjs papers.json` — encodes the E1/E2 ladder (name + citation + ≤4 arXiv ids), paces searches, rewrites the result file per paper |
| Download + score the code you found | see `references/code-scoring-rubric.md`: shallow-clone hygiene (verify HEAD + file count), measured-vs-judged rubric, and the four measurement traps |
| Affiliation (NOT in abstract) | `arxiv.org/html/<id>v<N>` — the affiliation block |
| Repo metadata | `api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo>` |
| Repo file tree | `api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo>/contents/` |
| Repo real commit history | `api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo>/commits?per_page=5` |
| Model-weights page | `huggingface.co/api/models/<owner>/<name>` |

**Escalate hosts, never declare a host dead.** `api.github.com`, `github.com`,
`raw.githubusercontent.com`, and the git protocol are *separate* channels with independent
reachability; any one may work while others fail, and reachability changes mid-session when a
proxy/VPN comes up. Probe each channel with one cheap request before giving up on the host.
Route around with whichever responds, and re-probe later in the session rather than trusting an
earlier failure.

## Procedure

1. **Pin the inclusion criteria before searching.** Write them as a numbered list the user can
   audit (e.g. subject, task domain, artifact required). Ambiguity in "small model" or "traditional
   ML" must be resolved *now* or the list will silently drift.
   When the question is "which of these papers fit *our* system", derive the criteria from that
   system's CODE, not from the paper taxonomy — and expect the user to add criteria in successive
   passes (fit → deployability → architectural compatibility). Keep ONE list file, add a column per
   layer, and print the funnel counts so the audit trail stays visible. Recipes and a worked example:
   `references/domain-fit-layering.md`.
2. **Harvest candidates from several faces**, not one query: arXiv Atom API with `abs:`/`ti:`/`cat:`
   booleans sorted by date; a multi-engine aggregator; plain web search; and non-English
   paper-note blogs, which surface venue-accepted work that English search misses.
   **Screen on whether the relevant experiment appears anywhere in the paper, not on how the
   paper frames itself.** A benchmark or dataset paper routinely contains the most comparable
   experiments to a methods request. Screening by title/framing silently drops these — one paper
   was misfiled as "no artifact" and mentioned in a single line, when it actually had the most
   complete artifact set of any paper found *and* reported the negative result that mattered most.
   Seed the candidate set and templates/evidence-graded-list.md carries the report skeleton.
3. **Verify metadata from the paper itself.** Fetch the abs page *and* the HTML full text. Get
   affiliations from the HTML affiliation block — **never infer an institution from an author's
   name or from a third-party summary.** Real example: a paper attributed by guesswork to a
   university was actually AWS AI Labs; the name-based guess was simply wrong.
4. **Verify every artifact claim with the GitHub API**, never with "the README fetched". See
   Pitfalls — this is the highest-value step and the easiest to get wrong. Existence is not
   identity: a live, non-empty repo that merely *cites* the paper (awesome-list, `*-daily`
   aggregator, book/course repo) is not its artifact. Grade only after the repo passes the
   identity ladder in `references/artifact-identity-and-filtering.md`.
5. **Assign an open-source grade**, highest obtainable first:
   `weights+code > code > dataset-only > "will release" > none found`.
   Grade on evidence, and record the evidence next to the grade.
6. **Rank and write.** Lead with a scannable summary table (one row per paper, with the grade
   column), then per-paper entries, then an explicit exclusions section, then a verification log.
   Once the list is final and the code is downloaded, `references/code-scoring-rubric.md` covers the
   follow-ups: one-folder bundling (`--depth 1 --single-branch`, verify HEAD + file count) and a
   measured-vs-judged scoring rubric with the four traps that make a first scoring pass wrong.
   **Before choosing dimensions, ask which question is being asked** — "does this fit our system"
   (porting fit) and "is this code any good" (code quality) are different rubrics, and picking without
   asking got a rubric rejected. For code quality the user's axes are fixed and equal-weight:
   架构合理性 · 鲁棒性 · 可维护性 · 易读性 · 可扩展性; each maps to measurable proxies in the reference.
7. **State the gap instead of padding.** If only one paper satisfies all criteria, say so and say
   the count. A padded list is worse than a short honest one.
   **Scaling to N projects (one isolated reader each)?** `references/subagent-fanout-and-synthesis.md`:
   write the baseline + coordinator + synthesis ledger BEFORE dispatching, make every prompt
   self-contained with a single writable report path, require incremental writing (the report is the
   breakpoint), and treat the merge as verification work — re-check load-bearing claims, recount
   summary tables against detail, and never let a self-assessed evidence score stand for a repo whose
   tests never ran.
   **A conflict analysis is not finished when it hands out dispositions.** Score every item on a
   conflict dimension with a stated pass line, delete what falls below it, and keep a one-line
   deletion log in the same file — that is what the user means by "从另一个维度打分并把低于及格线的
   排除和删掉". Run the coverage self-check (items = sum of group sizes) before scoring.
8. **Survey (or awesome-list) → domain-filtered list?** Follow
   `references/survey-to-domain-mapping.md`: pin the target system's axes from its CODE first, map
   survey sections → citations mechanically, then verify every annotation against the abstract and
   correct title/year from primary metadata before filtering by obtainability.

## Pitfalls

- **HTTP 200 on a raw README does NOT prove a repo has code.** A 9-byte README (`# AceGRPO`)
  fetches perfectly. This produced a wrong "code available" verdict that survived one round of
  review. Judge content, not reachability:
  - `size: 0` **or** `pushed_at == created_at` ⇒ empty repo; `contents/` returns
    `{"message":"This repository is empty."}`
  - only `.gitignore` + a tiny README ⇒ placeholder, no implementation
  - commits worth reading: `"Initial commit"` → `"Public release"` timelines corroborate that
    weights/artifacts really shipped, and the commit author should match a paper author
- **A repo URL printed in a paper is not evidence of code.** Two papers here published a GitHub
  link; both repos were empty. Conversely, a paper whose abs page carries *no* link may still have
  a working repo discoverable by author search — absence of a link is equally weak evidence.
- **Citing the paper ≠ being its artifact (the expensive one).** "README contains the arXiv ID" also
  matches awesome-lists, `arxiv-daily` aggregators and course repos — `huangjia2019/agent-design-patterns`,
  `SanDiegoMachineLearning/talks`, `joheras/Lecturas`, `Marontis/agentic-engineering` (106 IDs) all passed
  it. Title-token overlap alone returns look-alikes (`ksm26/LLMs-as-Operating-Systems-Agent-Memory` for
  MemGPT instead of `cpacker/MemGPT`). Working test: repo name contains the system name **and** README
  cites the paper **and** the README holds ≤4 distinct arXiv IDs. Productised repos (MemGPT/OpenHands/
  AutoGen) fail the citation leg after their READMEs were rewritten — keep them, but as a separate tier.
- **Third-party notes are not the paper.** A code URL copied from a paper-note blog had no
  counterpart in the paper's own abs page. Mark provenance per claim: paper text vs third party.
- **Affiliation is not in the abstract.** If you only fetched the abs page, you do not know the
  institution. Write "not verified" rather than guessing.
- **Do not stop at "not reachable" when a proxy may exist.** Ask the user to bring up their
  proxy/VPN, then re-probe; the reachable set can change within one session and unlock an entire
  verification pass that was previously blocked.
- **Never launch a verification subagent for domains whose reachability you have not confirmed.**
  Otherwise it burns its whole run on unreachable hosts and must be interrupted. Walk one probe
  yourself first, then delegate — and give the subagent the channel that actually works.
- **Verify the verifier's method, once it works.** Re-check earlier "confirmed" verdicts with the
  newly available channel — several will flip.
- **Long-running verification subagents can stall** on network-bound work. Interrupt and do the
  checks inline over a channel you have already proven, rather than waiting indefinitely.

## Verification

The report is done when, for every entry, you can point to (a) a fetched source for each
affiliation and numeric claim, and (b) an API-level artifact verdict. Re-read your own grade
column while asking "did I confirm *content*, or only that a URL resolves?" If any grade rests on
URL resolution alone, it is not yet verified. Then append a verification-log section listing
corrections you made, so the next reader can see what changed and why.

# Manual Test Plan Authoring

Write a step-by-step manual test procedure that a human operator (or a non-specialist tester) executes against a
running system to prove each功能项 is *present and does something*, not whether the output is good.
It does NOT grade defects (`codebase-defect-audit`) and does NOT survey what exists (`codebase-inventory-survey`).
The deliverable is a procedure document whose every step is copy-pasteable in the operator's own environment.

## When to Use

- "把每一项功能生成一套手动测试方案" / "给测试同学一份可照做的操作手册"
- A verification report or acceptance sheet needs a reproducible "how to observe this" section per capability
- The test surface is constrained (chat only, no settings UI, air-gapped box) and the steps must fit it
- Any request where the reader runs the steps, not the agent

## Prerequisites

- The code that implements the features (this is where the *reachable surface* comes from).
- The exact environment the steps will run in: which client, which UI, whether config/CLI exists at all.
- Read-only access to a live instance of that environment when you can get it — one probe beats three guesses.

## Procedure

1. **Derive the reachable surface from code before writing a single step.** Enumerate, per feature:
   the chat/CLI entry point, the keys it actually accepts, and what is only reachable through a
   settings UI or a config file. Steps that name an unreachable surface are worse than missing steps:
   the operator gets stuck and reports a false defect against the product.
2. **Budget the granularity to evidence, not to features.** One scenario per feature group, 3–6 steps each,
   each step being {what to send, what to expect}. If a step's observation needs a file the operator cannot open,
   replace it with a chat read ("读一下 <path>") or a status command.
3. **Write expectations as the artifact's own words** (tool receipt text, command reply, file field), quoted
   verbatim where it matters; keep them short. Say "回执文案以实际为准，语义一致即算命中" once instead of
   guessing every string.
4. **Run every command you ship, in the target environment's own shell, before shipping it.** Capture the real
   output; then write the expectation next to the command. Two traps that only show up when you run it:
   the tool silently operates on a *different* instance/profile unless you set the environment variables the
   deployment uses, and a flag may be documented but require an extra switch to actually print.
5. **List the unreachable items explicitly as 未测** with (a) why they are unreachable here, (b) the exact
   configuration or permission that would make them testable, (c) any partial substitute reading that the
   reachable steps still give. Never fold them into the pass column.
6. **Give one consolidated document.** Operators execute from one file; split only if the reader set differs.

# npm Package Publishing

Publish a JavaScript package to the npm registry either interactively from a local
machine or unattended from CI with OIDC trusted publishing, and diagnose a CI
publish that fails *after* the identity step already succeeded. It does not cover
registry signup, scope/org administration, or non-npm registries.

## When to Use

- "publish this package", "cut a release", "bump and publish"
- A GitHub Actions publish job fails with `E404 Not Found - PUT https://registry.npmjs.org/<pkg>`
- `npm publish` throws `EOTP` and only shows a URL with the challenge masked as `***`
- Setting up or auditing trusted publishing (`npm trust ...`)
- Deciding whether a read taken right after publishing is trustworthy yet

## Prerequisites

- npm ≥ 11.5.1 for trusted publishing (CI images often ship older; see step 2).
- `id-token: write` permission on the publishing job.
- A bound trusted publisher: repo + workflow filename (+ environment if used).
- For interactive publishing: a real console window (see Pitfalls) and the
  publisher's 2FA device. A security key / fingerprint has no 6-digit code to type.

## How to Run

Trusted publishing from CI is a one-time bind plus a tag push:

```bash
npm trust github <pkg> --file .github/workflows/publish.yml \
  --repo <owner>/<repo> [--env <environment>] --allow-publish -y
git tag v1.2.3 && git push origin v1.2.3     # triggers the workflow
```

**When the tag push itself is what fails, the API is the other door.** If `git push`
dies with `OpenSSL SSL_connect: SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL` or `Failed to connect to github.com
port 443` after ~21 s, test the API before blaming the network: `gh auth status` and
`gh run list` speak to `api.github.com` and routinely keep working while
`github.com:443` is blocked. Any workflow declaring `workflow_dispatch:` can then be
started with no tag at all:

```bash
gh workflow run publish.yml --ref main      # publishes the version on that ref
```

This path publishes whatever `package.json` says on that ref, so the tag becomes a
marker you push afterwards — which is exactly the situation that exposes the duplicate
guard in Pitfalls. Both doors are equivalent to the workflow; pick the one that works.

Interactive, from a console npm can actually open a browser out of (Windows):

```powershell
Start-Process cmd.exe -ArgumentList '/k', 'npm publish --access public'
```

## Quick Reference

| Action | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Bind a GitHub trusted publisher | `npm trust github <pkg> --file <wf> --repo <o/r> -y` |
| Inspect the binding | `npm trust list <pkg>` |
| Revoke by id | `npm trust revoke <pkg> --id=<uuid>` |
| What will be packed | `npm pack --dry-run` |
| Live versions | `npm view <pkg> versions dist-tags` |
| Watch the run | `gh run list --limit 5` / `gh run view <id> --log` |
| Manage explicit staging | `npm stage list / approve / reject` |

## Procedure

1. **Confirm the name and version are still free.** A published version is
   immutable — you bump it, you never overwrite it. Create a brand-new package
   name before pushing the tag that triggers its first publish. Publish bytes
   from the run's own artifacts, never a hand-assembled copy.
2. **Make the runner's npm new enough.** `npm install -g npm@latest` in the job
   and echo `npm --version`; setup-node's bundled npm can sit below 11.5.1, where
   trusted publishing silently cannot engage.
3. **Blank the static token on the publish step.** `actions/setup-node` with
   `registry-url:` writes an `.npmrc` and populates `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN` from
   `github.token`. npm then takes the static-token path instead of exchanging the
   OIDC token, and the registry rejects the write:

   ```yaml
   - name: Publish
     env:
       NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: ''
     run: npm publish --access public --provenance
   ```

4. **Read the failing log for what SUCCEEDED too.** In the same run,
   `Signed provenance statement ... from GitHub Actions` and `Provenance
   statement published to transparency log` prove the OIDC identity was
   accepted. That rules out "trusted publishing is not configured" and narrows
   the fault to the registry write itself.
5. **Change one suspected cause, then diff the error text.** Compare the new
   failure against the previous one verbatim. A byte-identical error falsifies
   the hypothesis — revert that guess instead of layering another patch on it.
6. **Read the registry twice.** npm 12 publishes in stages: `npm publish` first
   creates a transient `0.0.0-stage` stub (`"stub": true`, description
   "Temporary package placeholder for staged publishing") and the real version
   lands about a minute later, so a single immediate read reports an intermediate
   state. `npm stage list/approve/reject` govern *explicit* staging only;
   auto-staged publishes need no approval. Don't just wait it out — read the
   registry **directly** (`https://registry.npmjs.org/<pkg>`) instead of through
   `npm view`, which can still hand back the pre-publish list seconds after the
   version lands (measured: version stamped `05:58:19Z`, `npm view` at `05:58:31Z`
   still reported the old `dist-tags`).
7. **Verify what actually shipped.** `npm pack --dry-run` against the `files`
   whitelist, then compare the registry `shasum`/`integrity` with the local build.
8. **Pull the published tarball back and diff it against the tree.** A local pack is
   not the released artifact:

   ```bash
   npm pack <pkg>@<version> --pack-destination "$TMP"   # downloads the published one
   # its sha1 must equal the registry's dist.shasum - that proves you are comparing it
   ```

   Then compare per file. **A worktree that keeps CRLF for some files while CI packs a
   fresh LF checkout yields a different tarball for identical content**, so a shasum
   mismatch against a *local* pack is expected, not alarming — normalise line endings
   and compare content. Measured: exactly two files differed, by their CR counts
   (338 + 871 bytes); every other file was byte-identical, and the CR delta matched
   `git ls-files --eol`'s `w/crlf` list exactly. State which files are `w/crlf` when you
   report this, and note that local packs are therefore not byte-reproducible.
9. **A review verdict covers only the commit it read.** If a shipped file moves after
   the review, either run another round or show the delta is inert:

   ```bash
   git diff -U0 <reviewed>..<released> -- <shipped paths>
   # strip lines starting with //, * or /* ; what remains must be the version line only
   ```

   Otherwise "it passed review" is an empty claim about the artifact. This is the
   release-side twin of "publish bytes from the run's own artifacts".

## Pitfalls

- **Predict that wall before spending a publish cycle on it: ask the channel whether it has a TTY.** In PowerShell, `[System.Console]::IsOutputRedirected` / `IsInputRedirected` answer it in one call (measured: both `True` on an agent-routed command channel). When both are true, `npm publish` on a package whose publisher requires 2FA **cannot** succeed — `otplease` throws `EOTP` and never reaches its browser branch — so the honest move is to stop after one attempt, report the capability finding as the blocker, hand over the exact two-command sequence (`npm publish` then `git tag v<ver> && git push origin v<ver>`), and let the human press it in a real console. Do not loop the same attempt; the channel cannot change mid-session, so retries are pure cost.
- **Bump, publish, and tag in that order — the tag records a published artifact, not an intention.** Measured near-miss: with `package.json` already at `0.1.8` and the registry still at `0.1.7`, tagging `v0.1.8` would have created a marker for a release that does not exist, and the local tree would claim "released" while the registry disagreed. Keeping the tag until the registry confirms keeps one source of truth (the registry) and makes an interrupted release resumable with no cleanup.
- **`EOTP` with no code prompt.** npm's `otplease` (`npm/lib/utils/auth.js`)
  runs `if (!process.stdin.isTTY || !process.stdout.isTTY) { throw err }`.
  Without a TTY it never reaches the "open a browser" branch: it prints the auth
  URL with the challenge masked as `***` and rethrows. Launch the publish from a
  real console — `Start-Process cmd.exe -ArgumentList '/k', '<cmd>'` — so npm can
  open the browser for a security-key / fingerprint tap. `npm trust list` needs
  the same treatment, and the masked URL is worthless for recovering by hand.
- **Confirm the next version from the registry, and the payload from a dry run — before you bump anything.** Measured on a package whose local tags stopped one release behind: `npm view <pkg> versions --json` listed `0.1.0 … 0.1.7` while the last local tag was `v0.1.7`, so the only legal next number was `0.1.8` (republishing an existing version is refused, and a lower one is worse). Pair it with `npm pack --dry-run`, which is the only cheap way to see what will actually ship: `files` globs are easy to trust and easy to get wrong — a new directory under a globbed path (`lib/ops/`) ships silently, while a file outside them (`cordis.patch.yml`) only ships if it is listed. Read the printed file list and byte count as the release artifact, not the git tree.
- **`E404` on PUT while provenance succeeded** almost always means the token path
  was taken instead of OIDC (step 3). It is not a scope, name, or
  metadata-field problem: adding `repository` / `homepage` / `bugs` does not
  change the error.
- **`E422` — provenance needs a PUBLIC source repo.** A private origin gets the
  write rejected with `Error verifying sigstore provenance bundle: Unsupported
  GitHub Actions source repository visibility: "private"`. Fix: drop
  `--provenance`. Do **not** also add `provenance=false` — npm only auto-enables
  provenance when the OIDC payload says `repository_visibility === 'public'`
  (`npm/lib/utils/oidc.js`), so a private repo is never auto-enabled. State the
  tradeoff plainly to the owner: private origin ⇒ no provenance on the tarball,
  and those two are mutually exclusive. Making the repo public is an
  outward-facing change — get explicit consent, never flip it to "fix" this.
- **A `repository` field is still read and validated** under trusted publishing,
  so keep it accurate even though no token is involved.
- **`files` is a whitelist, not a filter.** Directories such as `design/`,
  `test/`, `tools/` do not ship unless listed; and a file that must ship but is
  not listed fails silently at install time, not at publish time.
- **A pattern-based count is a claim about the pattern, not the world.** Before
  "correcting" a count from a grep, widen the pattern and re-count.
- **Re-publishing a shipped version is a no-op, not a failure — and that is a trap
  unless you pair it.** Push a tag *after* a manual dispatch and the tag-triggered run
  fails with `npm error You cannot publish over the previously published versions:
  <v>.` The wrong fix is "remember the order"; the right one is two guards that only
  work together:

  ```yaml

      expected="v$(node -p "require('./package.json').version")"

      fi

    env: { NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: '' }
    run: |
      version="$(node -p "require('./package.json').version")"
  ```

# npm Package Publishing

Publish a JavaScript package to the npm registry either interactively from a local
machine or unattended from CI with OIDC trusted publishing, and diagnose a CI
publish that fails *after* the identity step already succeeded. It does not cover
registry signup, scope/org administration, or non-npm registries.

- "publish this package", "cut a release", "bump and publish"
- A GitHub Actions publish job fails with `E404 Not Found - PUT https://registry.npmjs.org/<pkg>`
- `npm publish` throws `EOTP` and only shows a URL with the challenge masked as `***`
- Setting up or auditing trusted publishing (`npm trust ...`)
- Deciding whether a read taken right after publishing is trustworthy yet

- npm ≥ 11.5.1 for trusted publishing (CI images often ship older; see step 2).
- `id-token: write` permission on the publishing job.
- A bound trusted publisher: repo + workflow filename (+ environment if used).
- For interactive publishing: a real console window (see Pitfalls) and the
  publisher's 2FA device. A security key / fingerprint has no 6-digit code to type.

Trusted publishing from CI is a one-time bind plus a tag push:

```bash
npm trust github <pkg> --file .github/workflows/publish.yml \
  --repo <owner>/<repo> [--env <environment>] --allow-publish -y
git tag v1.2.3 && git push origin v1.2.3     # triggers the workflow
```

**When the tag push itself is what fails, the API is the other door.** If `git push`
dies with `OpenSSL SSL_connect: SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL` or `Failed to connect to github.com
port 443` after ~21 s, test the API before blaming the network: `gh auth status` and
`gh run list` speak to `api.github.com` and routinely keep working while
`github.com:443` is blocked. Any workflow declaring `workflow_dispatch:` can then be
started with no tag at all:

```bash
gh workflow run publish.yml --ref main      # publishes the version on that ref
```

This path publishes whatever `package.json` says on that ref, so the tag becomes a
marker you push afterwards — which is exactly the situation that exposes the duplicate
guard in Pitfalls. Both doors are equivalent to the workflow; pick the one that works.

Interactive, from a console npm can actually open a browser out of (Windows):

```powershell
Start-Process cmd.exe -ArgumentList '/k', 'npm publish --access public'
```
